title: Scientists Built 'Lifeless Earth' Simulation to Stop JWST From Crying Wolf on Alien Life
excerpt: University of Washington researchers have published a 5-billion-year computational simulation of Earth without life, validated against 19 real planetary properties, that gives JWST and the planned Habitable Worlds Observatory their first rigorous null hypothesis for distinguishing geology from
content:
Imagine announcing to the world that you've found signs of life on another planet — and then discovering that a volcano could explain everything you saw. That is not a hypothetical scenario; it is the credibility risk that has shadowed every tentative biosignature claim JWST has produced. And until last month, scientists had no rigorous way to rule it out.

A team at the University of Washington has now built the tool they were missing. In a paper published September 18 in The Planetary Science Journal, lead author Samantha Gilbert-Janizek and her collaborators describe a comprehensive computational model of Earth — constructed without any life whatsoever — that simulates five billion years of purely geological planetary evolution. The result, now circulating widely since the university's November 2 press release and covered by Space.com on November 8, is what may be the most scientifically rigorous null hypothesis yet devised for interpreting the atmospheric spectra that JWST is collecting from rocky worlds beyond our solar system.

The timing is pointed. Last year, a landmark paper in PNAS by MIT planetary scientist Sara Seager and colleagues concluded that "with JWST, we may never be able to definitively claim the discovery of a biosignature gas in an exoplanet atmosphere." The Gilbert-Janizek model is a direct response to that methodological impasse: it establishes, for the first time, a validated computational baseline for what a dead planet's atmosphere looks like — so that researchers can say with quantified confidence whether an observed atmosphere exceeds what geology can produce.

Why the False Positive Problem Is Real, Not Theoretical

Astronomers hunting for life on exoplanets face a genuinely hard problem. The primary tool available for the job — atmospheric spectroscopy, which parses the chemical fingerprint of starlight filtered through a planet's air — cannot distinguish a biologist from a basalt formation by itself. Gases that life produces abundantly, such as oxygen, methane, and nitrous oxide, can also be generated through purely geological processes: volcanic outgassing, photochemical reactions driven by UV radiation, mineral-water interactions at the seafloor.

The simultaneous presence of oxygen and methane is a canonical biosignature candidate. Life replenishes both continuously on Earth, preventing the two reactive gases from neutralizing each other. But the same pairing could, in principle, arise on a geologically active world under certain abiotic conditions. Without a principled way to rule out the geological explanation, any detection claim collapses under its own uncertainty.

This is not an abstract concern. The exoplanet K2-18b became global news in 2023 when Cambridge astronomers tentatively detected dimethyl sulfide (DMS) — a gas produced on Earth almost exclusively by marine organisms — in its atmosphere using JWST. A stronger claim followed in April 2025. But a NASA-led reanalysis found no conclusive evidence; independent spectral fitting showed that propyne and other abiotic hydrocarbons provide equally good — or better — matches to the same data. The story of K2-18b is the story of exactly why the biosignature field needs a formal null hypothesis before it can responsibly claim to have found an inhabited world.

JWST is already gathering transmission spectra from TRAPPIST-1 planets and other rocky habitable-zone worlds. As those datasets accumulate over the coming years, the scientific community needs a defensible standard for what an uninhabited atmosphere looks like. The lifeless-Earth model provides it.

Building the Lifeless Planet

The University of Washington team's approach was to construct the most complete abiotic Earth ever modeled. Their simulation — running from roughly 50 million years after Earth's formation through approximately 500 million years into its future, a span of about five billion years — tracks the geochemical coevolution of every major planetary reservoir: core, mantle, crust, ocean surface, and atmosphere, continuously and simultaneously.

The model is built on VPLanet planet evolution code developed in the Barnes lab over more than a decade. Prior versions of the model tracked the core, mantle, crust, and stellar radiation inputs, but stopped short of connecting those interior processes to the ocean surface and the atmosphere above. Gilbert-Janizek's contribution was to close that gap, adding volatile cycling through the surface and atmosphere to complete the planetary loop.

The specific additions drew on established physics from multiple subdisciplines. The carbon cycle uses the climate-stabilizing framework from Foley (2015), which tracks CO₂ mass across the mantle, plate, and surface reservoirs. The deep water cycle uses Seales and Lenardic (2020) to track H₂O across the mantle and surface. At each timestep, surface carbon and water are partitioned between the atmosphere and the ocean by enforcing chemical equilibrium at the air-water boundary — the same equilibrium that governs Earth's real carbonate chemistry. No biological process participates at any stage.

The result is a self-consistent, fully coupled account of how a habitable, geologically active, Sun-orbiting rocky planet evolves chemically over geological time — driven purely by physics, not biology.

"This model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets," said lead author Gilbert-Janizek, who completed the research as a doctoral student at UW and is now a postdoctoral fellow at UC Riverside. "When we interpret observations of an exoplanet's atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface."

Nineteen Tests, Zero Life

The critical question for any model is whether it actually works. Here the researchers applied a stringent benchmark: the lifeless Earth simulation must accurately reproduce observable properties of the real Earth — a planet whose geology, while influenced by life at the margins, is dominated by the same physical processes the model is designed to capture.

The model was validated against 19 independent planetary parameters spanning the entire Earth system. The confirmed list includes atmospheric CO₂ and H₂O concentrations, surface temperature, albedo, ocean mass, upper-mantle temperature, and upper-mantle heat flow, among others — all reproduced within measurement uncertainties after 4.5 billion years of simulated evolution, without tuning any biological factors into the calculation.

This validation step matters as much as the model itself. A lifeless-Earth baseline is only useful as a null hypothesis if it is demonstrably realistic. Because the model matches 19 measured properties of a world we can examine directly, researchers can trust that the abiotic spectra it produces reflect genuine planetary chemistry rather than computational artifacts.

"Dr. Gilbert-Janizek's work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe," said senior author Rory Barnes, an associate professor of astronomy at UW. "After more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr. Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earth's core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate."

From Spectra to Null Hypothesis

The model's geochemical states can be fed into radiative transfer codes to generate synthetic spectra — in effect, what a distant telescope would observe when looking at a lifeless but habitable Earth at any point in its five-billion-year history. The team produced synthetic reflected-light spectra covering the 0.2 to 2.0 micrometer range — spanning ultraviolet through near-infrared — for both the inhabited Earth and the abiotic Earth at 4.5 billion years, allowing direct comparison of what biology adds to a planet's spectral signature.

These synthetic spectra represent the abiotic baseline: the full range of spectral signatures that geology alone can produce on a world like ours. When a real exoplanet observation arrives — say, a JWST transmission spectrum showing an infrared absorption feature suggesting CO₂ and CH₄ — researchers can compare it against this library of abiotic spectra. If the observed feature falls within the abiotic range, the geological explanation cannot be ruled out. If it lies clearly outside what the lifeless model can produce, the case for biology strengthens considerably.

This is precisely how null hypotheses are supposed to function in science. The model does not claim to identify inhabited worlds; it establishes the baseline against which any such claim must be measured.

A Tool for JWST and Its Successors

JWST is operating at the frontier of what current technology can resolve in exoplanet atmospheres. Its transmission spectroscopy capabilities are powerful, but most rocky habitable-zone planets remain at the edge of detectability, and as the Seager et al. findings underscored, its noise floor may preclude definitive biosignature confirmation even under best-case conditions.

The lifeless-Earth model is designed to serve that effort now — and to scale naturally to the more capable observatories coming next. The researchers specifically highlight the proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, a next-generation NASA flagship mission designed to characterize rocky planets in reflected light around nearby Sun-like stars. For HWO, the abiotic baseline will be even more critical: the observatory is expected to gather reflected-light spectra in the same 0.2 to 2.0 micrometer wavelength range the model already covers, dramatically expanding both biosignature signal access and false-positive risk.

"Realizing the ambitious goals of a telescope like the Habitable Worlds Observatory requires decades of work across many generations of scientists," Gilbert-Janizek said. "I'm so grateful to join this lineage and one day pass the torch to the next generation so that we can continue chipping away at this question of whether or not we are alone in the universe."

The model's architecture is designed to be customizable. By adjusting initial conditions — planetary mass, stellar irradiance, interior composition, and water inventory — the team can generate abiotic baselines for rocky exoplanets that differ from Earth in systematically varied ways. That flexibility will allow astronomers to tailor the null hypothesis to whatever specific world JWST or HWO happens to be studying, rather than applying a single Earth-calibrated baseline to every rocky planet regardless of its actual properties.

Closing the Gap in Biosignature Science

Astrobiology has sometimes been characterized as a field searching for answers before it has fully defined the questions. The University of Washington model is a direct response to that critique: a rigorous effort to formalize, in computational terms, exactly what the absence of life looks like across geological time.

No true abiotic control site exists on Earth today — life has permeated the planet's chemistry so thoroughly that there is no pristine corner of the geosphere untouched by biology. That is what makes a validated computational model so valuable. It provides the control experiment that nature itself cannot offer.

The researchers note that future iterations could extend the model to explore the abiotic production of additional candidate biosignature gases, including methane, and to survey a broader range of planetary and stellar conditions. Each such expansion widens the library of null-hypothesis scenarios that future observations must be tested against.

For the moment, the existence of a validated, whole-planet, 5-billion-year abiotic Earth model represents meaningful progress in one of the most consequential scientific endeavors of the century. The search for life elsewhere is proceeding at speed. The tools for not being fooled by geology are finally beginning to catch up.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a biosignature, and why do scientists worry about false positives?

A biosignature is any chemical or physical signal that provides evidence of past or present life. In exoplanet science, researchers look for gases in planetary atmospheres — such as oxygen, methane, and dimethyl sulfide — that life produces in large quantities. The false-positive problem arises because many of these same gases can also be produced by geological processes, UV photochemistry, or specific atmospheric conditions that have nothing to do with biology. Without a validated baseline for what a dead planet can produce, any biosignature detection is scientifically incomplete.

How does the 'lifeless Earth' model actually work?

The model is built on the VPLanet code platform developed at the University of Washington. It simulates the coupled evolution of Earth's core, mantle, crust, ocean surface, and atmosphere over five billion years, tracking the movement of carbon and water between reservoirs using established geochemical equations — with no biological processes included. At each point in time, the model can generate synthetic spectra that show what a distant telescope would observe. Researchers can then compare real exoplanet observations against this library to test whether a signal requires life to explain it.

Can JWST already detect signs of life on other planets?

JWST is powerful enough to detect certain atmospheric gases in exoplanet atmospheres, and it has already gathered intriguing — if contested — data on planets like K2-18b. However, a landmark 2025 paper in PNAS by Sara Seager and colleagues concluded that JWST's noise floor may prevent it from ever definitively confirming a biosignature gas on its own. The lifeless-Earth model is designed to sharpen the interpretation of whatever signals JWST does detect, by providing a rigorous baseline for what geology alone can produce.

What is the Habitable Worlds Observatory, and when will it launch?

The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) is NASA's next planned flagship space telescope, specifically designed to search for life on rocky Earth-like planets around nearby Sun-like stars. Unlike JWST, which primarily studies planets as they transit their host stars, HWO is designed to image planets directly using a coronagraph — allowing it to study reflected starlight rather than transmission spectra. HWO is currently in pre-formulation development, with a concept review targeted for the late 2020s and launch currently anticipated in the 2040s. The lifeless-Earth model's synthetic spectra already cover HWO's planned 0.2 to 2.0 micrometer wavelength range.

What would it take to actually confirm life on another planet?

No single observation is likely to suffice. The emerging scientific consensus is that confirming life will require: a positive detection of a potential biosignature gas; a validated abiotic model showing the signal cannot be explained by geological or photochemical processes alone; independent confirmation across multiple instruments and observations; and a statistical framework (such as Bayesian inference) that quantifies the probability of a biological origin given all available evidence. The lifeless-Earth model provides the validated abiotic component — one of the essential elements that has been missing.
